title: Cause and effect
subtitle: cause, produce, generate, stem from
summary: Choose between cause, produce, give and generate by their collocations, and use the other cause words - provoke, spark, precipitate, bring about, stem from - with the right prepositions.

lesson.heading: The four main cause verbs and what they go with
rows: cause
usually negative results and situations
sadness/unhappiness; (a lot of) trouble/problems; an illness, e.g. pneumonia; a disaster / an accident
produce
neutral, more concrete results; formal
a report; statistics/figures; good results; evidence
give
positive or negative; less formal than cause
(a lot of) pleasure/happiness; a reason/motivation for something; (a lot of) trouble; good results
generate
formal; often where people must do more than usual, and in computing; sometimes slightly negative
revenue/income/money; complaints / extra work / controversy; graphics/documents; interest/enthusiasm/publicity

lesson.heading: The four verbs in sentences
lesson.text: Learn each verb through its collocations. **Cause** takes the bad news, **produce** the concrete output, **give** the personal experience, good or bad, and **generate** the money, the interest and the computer file.

examples.text: The new computer system has **caused** us a lot of problems.
Cooking the dish for a long time at a very low heat **produces** the best results.
Our dog has **given** us a lot of pleasure over the years.
This car is **giving** me so much trouble, I'm going to get rid of it.
It's going to be difficult to **generate** sufficient interest in the project.

left.label: cause / give
left.text: Often used for things that happen without anybody doing anything.
examples: His stomach cancer was **caused** by exposure to radiation.

right.label: produce / generate
right.text: Usually suggest some sort of intervention by people.
examples: His presentation **generated** a lot of interest in the project.
Scientists can **produce** statistics and figures that prove almost anything.

lesson.heading: Sudden causes and gradual ones
lesson.text: **Provoke** is ideal for negative responses and emotions. **Precipitate** and **spark** mean to cause quickly and suddenly - perfect for things that explode into life. **Bring about**, by contrast, means to produce gradually.

examples.text: The news **provoked** a feeling of despair in everyone.
The book **provoked** a lot of anger amongst female readers.
The invention of the car **brought about** great changes in society.

lesson.heading: Looking back at the cause
lesson.text: To **result in** something is to produce it; to **stem from** something is to be a result of it. **Grounds for** something is a cause or reason, and an argument **based on** data has been developed as a result of that data.

examples.text: Your action has **resulted in** a formal complaint from a member of the public.
His problems **stem from** his difficult childhood.
Have you any **grounds for** suspecting him?
My argument is **based on** the available data.

lesson.heading: The prepositions to fix in your memory
rows: grounds for
I have good grounds for believing that he is lying.
based on
My suspicions are based on what I saw with my own eyes.
implications for
The government's decision has serious implications for the economy.
stem from
His fear of flying stems from a film he once saw.
result in
All her hard work has resulted in success.
bring about
The riots will probably bring about a change of government.
be caused by
A considerable amount of damage was caused by the tornado.
lesson.note: If a proposal has implications for something, it is likely to cause certain results there.

lesson.text: **Result** only ever collocates with **in** - hard work **results in** success, never ~~results to~~ success.

exercises.prompt: We need to ___ a list of names and addresses by six o'clock tonight.
exercises.hint: (the usual verb with list, report, figures)
exercises.explanation: Produce is the most frequent collocation with list; generate is possible in more technical contexts.

exercises.prompt: Her death was ___ by a sign falling from a shop front in the heavy winds.
exercises.explanation: Cause collocates with negative situations, and is used where nobody deliberately intervened.

exercises.prompt: His stupidity ___ in none of us being able to get home that night.
exercises.hint: (past tense; the verb that takes in)
exercises.explanation: Result is the only possibility here - it collocates with in.

exercises.prompt: Your letters have ___ me so much pleasure. Please don't stop writing them.
exercises.hint: (the less formal verb, used for positive results)
exercises.explanation: Give is less formal than cause and can be used for positive results such as pleasure and happiness.

exercises.prompt: The book ___ a lot of anger amongst female readers.
exercises.explanation: Provoke is ideal for negative responses and emotions.

exercises.prompt: The decision by the government to relax the regulations has ___ a lot of investment in the poorer regions.
exercises.explanation: Generate is used for revenue, income, interest and publicity, and suggests human intervention.

exercises.prompt: The Governor's remarks almost ___ a full-scale war between the two regions.
exercises.explanation: Spark and precipitate are ideal for things that happen suddenly and violently.

exercises.prompt: I don't necessarily want to ___ a crisis, but I have some bad news to tell you all.
exercises.explanation: Precipitate means to cause something suddenly, and is more dramatic than cause or bring about.

exercises.prompt: The invention of the car ___ great changes in society.
exercises.explanation: Bring about means to produce gradually, over a long period.

exercises.prompt: I have good grounds ___ believing that he is lying.
exercises.explanation: Grounds for something is a cause or reason for it.

exercises.prompt: My suspicions are based ___ what I saw with my own eyes.
exercises.explanation: An argument or suspicion is based on the evidence that provides its basis.

exercises.prompt: His fear of flying stems ___ a film he once saw.
exercises.explanation: To stem from something is to be a result of it.

exercises.prompt: The government's decision has serious implications ___ the economy.
exercises.explanation: Implications for something means it is likely to cause certain results there.

exercises.statement: Produce and generate usually suggest that people have intervened in some way.
exercises.explanation: Correct - cause and give are the verbs used when things happen without anyone doing anything.

exercises.statement: We would normally say 'The dog caused us a lot of pleasure over the years.'
exercises.explanation: Cause collocates with negative results. Say: The dog has given us a lot of pleasure over the years.

exercises.prompt: Match each cause with its effect, using the verb suggested.

pairs.right: a number of serious accidents this week

pairs.left: My old car has given me ...
pairs.right: endless problems and a lot of expense

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this with 'caused': Because of the crash on the motorway, all traffic is being severely delayed.
exercises.answer: The crash on the motorway has caused all traffic to be severely delayed
exercises.explanation: Cause takes the pattern cause something to do something, and collocates with negative situations.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this with 'brought about': There were many flight cancellations because of bad weather.
exercises.answer: The bad weather brought about many flight cancellations
exercises.explanation: Bring about means to produce a result, typically gradually.
